fields.description: Beyond the sweep's fixed schedules: seeded generation of schedules over several machines and actors, competing writers interleaved, and faults anywhere and repeated: lost replies, stalls, refusals, partitions (a machine cut off from the remote for a span while others work), and crashes at every boundary. The oracle is the property, not the count. Accepted ownership survives failures: once the remote accepted a claim at generation g, every machine settles on that owner or a newer generation, never an older one, and a lost acknowledgement never makes a second owner. A stale owner cannot invalidate a newer claim: a release, close, update or takeover by an owner whose claim was superseded never changes the issue's owner or the fields the claim guards, on any machine. Also: at most one confirmed owner; generations monotone; exports, show and claims converge after settling; every answer consistent with what the remote holds.
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- A seed reproduces its schedule; a failing schedule is shrunk to a minimal one and reported with its steps.
- Coverage evidence: the run counts, per operation, fault and boundary, the schedules where the fault fired, and fails when a combination was never exercised.
- A small budget runs in the fast suite; the nightly job (.github/workflows/rust-nightly.yml) runs 10^5 to 10^6 schedules.
fields.title: Ownership explored over generated schedules: accepted claims survive, stale owners cannot win

fields.description: docs/RUST-PORT.md §4.8. proptest properties in the fast suite: replay is invariant under delivery order, and JSON round-trips in every dialect bead writes. cargo-fuzz targets for the JSON parser, the segment reader and the Beads importer, in fuzz/ (its own workspace, as Cargo.toml notes), run nightly with a time budget, their corpus seeded from real exports that are never checked in.
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- The properties run in the fast suite.
- The three targets build and run nightly within the budget; a crash fails the job and keeps its input.
fields.title: Fuzzing: replay and JSON properties, cargo-fuzz targets run nightly

fields.description: A cargo llvm-cov report over the suites (the simulation's runs too, once they exist), made nightly as an artifact and by an xtask command, so that protocol code no test reaches is visible. What it shows untested in the ownership protocol is filed as issues.
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- The report is produced nightly and on demand.
- Untested ownership-protocol code it shows is filed as issues.
fields.title: A coverage report of the suites

data.text: Split on 2026-10-11 (maintainer's plan: make the correctness evidence stronger before changing the protocol): .1 the Remote seam with the in-memory remote, conformant with git (the trait lands with its second implementation, §2.3i); .2 the sweep's 660 schedules over it, checked against the real-git sweep; .3 generated schedules with faults anywhere, judged by the properties that matter: accepted ownership survives failures, and stale owners cannot invalidate newer claims; .4 fuzzing; .5 coverage. Schedule counts alone are not the goal: every run shows which faults fired where. The real-git sweep, its variants and the stress models stay the end-to-end check.

fields.description:
Decision of 2026-10-11, from assessing a proposal to supersede segment rotation with published checkpoints, a bounded recent journal, an archive of older history and a local state cache. The proposal's target is right: a command, a sync and a fresh machine's first fetch should cost in proportion to the current state plus the recent changes, not to the whole history. Its order is not: checkpoints come last, after two cheap fixes and a local projection, because a published checkpoint needs a history boundary and a format 2, and nothing measured needs them yet.

Why checkpoints are not first:
- README's decisions table and docs/REVIEWING.md §2 chose "segment rotation only" deliberately and named the next step: a persisted projection is the obvious next step if that ever matters.
- Measured on this repository's own tracker on 2026-10-11: 250 issues, 762 events, 2.6 MB of journal, 262 events a day at the busiest, `bead list --json` in 10 ms and 7 MB, every file hashed by git in 14 ms, 259 commits on the remote ref. The latest field values and the comments are 56% of the journal's bytes, so a checkpoint of this tracker would be about half its journal: the growth is issue text, which a checkpoint keeps. Reclaiming more means forgetting closed issues, a retention decision that changes what export returns.
- At that rate a year is about 95,000 events and 320 MB. Replay stays near 0.15 s. Memory reaches about 1 GB with today's representation, which roll-dih8.11 fixes. Hashing every file under the store lock reaches about a second, twice per write, which remembering the blob ids of full segments fixes. Only the disk and a fresh machine's first fetch need checkpoints.
- A checkpoint carries more than the state. Registers, tag sets, retracted sets and claim generations are keyed by event id; write_register, dependency and label removal and the claim rules ask saw_at(late event, old id); a new event's deps are the frontier, so any old event can be a cause. A checkpoint therefore carries an index over all history, about 100 bytes an event, and "proportional to current state" is an overstatement.
- "Continuation from a checkpoint agrees with full replay" cannot hold in general. Two concurrent creates that minted one key go to whichever replay applies second in canonical order, so a late older-id create keeps the key in a full replay and is renamed in a continuation; claim history, comments and issue order are replay order. The property a checkpoint can offer is that every machine continuing from the same checkpoint agrees, which makes the checkpoint canonical and the archive no longer an oracle. That is a history boundary, to decide explicitly before any format work. A rolled-over tracker also ends the python-0.1.0 rollback, and the fork, quarantine and chain-break findings in docs/FINDINGS.md assume every raw record is present.

The order, one child each; format 1 stays frozen through the first four:
1. roll-dih8.11: a compact event representation, for memory. No format change.
2. Sync hashes only the active segment, for time under the store lock. No format change. Independent of 1.
3. A rebuildable local projection, for every command's time: exact for local writes, full replay the fallback. Waits for 1 and 2.
4. The history-boundary decision, in docs/REVIEWING.md §2. Waits for 3's measurements.
5. Published checkpoints, an archive ref and a format-2 rollover, only when a real tracker's published tree or first fetch hurts. Waits for 3 and 4.
6. Retention as a separate, explicit policy. Waits for 5.
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- Children 1 to 4 are closed.
- Children 5 and 6 are closed, or stay open with the measured trigger that would start them written in each.
- A read command on a 200,000-event history costs in proportion to the state, and a sync in proportion to the state and the changes since the last one, recorded by cargo xtask timing.
- README.md, docs/REVIEWING.md §2 and docs/FINDINGS.md say what changed; the fast baseline is green; the changes are on main.
fields.title: Keep routine cost proportional to current state plus recent changes

fields.description:
Every write that publishes (a sync, a claim, a close) hashes every journal segment and every attempt file of the store with `git hash-object --stdin-paths`, in Link::local_blobs (crates/beadroll-sync/src/link/write.rs): once in merge (link/merge.rs) and once more in tree (link/publish.rs), both under the store lock. On this repository's tracker that is 14 ms for 2.6 MB of segments and 87 attempt files today; at its busiest rate of 262 events a day, about 900 KiB a day, it reaches about a second per hashing within a year, twice per write, and it grows with the history while a write changes one file.

A segment that rotated (Journal::active_segment in crates/beadroll-store/src/journal.rs rotates at BEAD_ROTATE_BYTES before an append, and a full segment is never appended to again) and an attempt file (written once, never changed) keep their blob ids. Remember them, keyed by path and length (repair_tail may shorten a full segment's torn tail, which the length shows), hash only the active segment and the files not remembered, and hash once per publish instead of twice. The last published commit's tree already names every file's blob id, so the memo may be read from it rather than kept beside the store; either way a remembered id that cannot be trusted (the length differs, the file is missing, the memo is unreadable) means hashing the file again. The published tree is byte for byte the one full hashing produces: a cost change inside beadroll-sync and beadroll-store, no format or protocol change, nothing new in the tree.

Step 2 of the epic; independent of step 1 (roll-dih8.11). Step 3, the projection, uses the same keys.
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- A publishing write hashes only the active segment, new attempt files and files whose length changed: a test observes it (the paths handed to hash-object, or the count of hashings) across a rotation, a repaired tail and a new claim.
- The tree published with the memo equals the tree published without it in those same cases, checked by a test.
- A missing, stale or unreadable memo is never trusted: the file is hashed again, with a test for each.
- cargo xtask timing's sync figure at 200,000 events does not grow with the number of full segments.
- CHANGELOG entry; the fast baseline and, since the link changed, ./check.sh --stress green.
fields.title: Sync hashes only the active segment: remember the blob ids of full segments and attempt files

fields.description:
Every command loads and replays the whole journal (view, load_journal and replay in crates/beadroll-core/src/journal.rs), and Link::merge (crates/beadroll-sync/src/link/merge.rs) replays once more to detect its own chain breaks: 8 ms at 10,000 events, 0.26 s at 200,000, and the memory of roll-dih8.11. docs/REVIEWING.md §2 records the choice ("no persisted projection") and README's known limits name a persisted projection as the obvious next step. This is that step: a cache, never a source.

The projection is the replayed State plus what settle needs (every event id with its content hash, each chain's last position, the accepted attempt ids), written beside the store (never half-written: the store's write rules) and keyed by what it was built from: each journal file's path and length, the blob ids step 2 remembers, the set of attempt files, the bead version and the format. A command whose files match reads it and never opens the journal; one whose files do not rebuilds it; a machine without one, or with one that is corrupt, truncated or from another version, replays as today. bead gives the same answers with and without it, and deleting it is safe at any moment.

Where it is exact and where it falls back:
- A local write appends events whose deps are the frontier (Tx, journal.heads()), so applying them to the projection is what replay does: O(new events).
- A merge whose new events are all causally after the frontier (one writer at a time, the common case) advances it the same way, and settle checks only the records the merge brought against the index.
- A merge that brings events concurrent with ones already applied can change what a replay would have done (register supersession through saw_at, key renames between concurrent creates in replay/apply/create.rs, the replay order of comments, claim history and issues), so after it the projection is rebuilt by full replay. How often that happens on real trackers is a number this step records, because step 4's decision needs it.

The oracle is replay and the tests are differential, as the port's were against Python: the stress models' and xtask's histories, replayed whole and through the projection in every interleaving of local writes and merges, equal state every time; failpoint tests for a crash while the projection is written; a test for each way it can be untrustworthy.

Step 3 of the epic. Waits for step 1 (the representation of State changes there) and step 2 (the same keys).
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- cargo xtask timing at 200,000 events: a read command (list, show, ready) with a projection in place costs in proportion to the state, not the events; a sync that merges N new events after the frontier costs in proportion to N and the state; cold, both cost what they do today.
- Differential tests over the stress models' histories: the state through the projection equals full replay after every local write and every merge, concurrent ones included, in every order.
- A corrupt, truncated, deleted or foreign-version projection is rebuilt, never trusted, with a test for each; a crash while it is written leaves the previous one or none.
- The fraction of merges on this repository's tracker that brought concurrent events is recorded here for step 4.
- docs/REVIEWING.md §2's "no persisted projection" row is replaced by this decision; README's known limit is updated; CHANGELOG entry; the fast baseline and ./check.sh --stress green.
fields.title: A rebuildable local projection: commands and merges stop replaying the whole journal

fields.description:
A published checkpoint makes a choice that rotation and a local projection never do: whether a machine with arbitrarily old offline work is always merged automatically, as today (the stress models and the protocol sweep pin it), or whether there is a supported history boundary behind which a machine must refresh and reconcile explicitly, its pending work preserved but not merged by itself.

Why the decision comes before any format work, and is not left to the implementation:
- Continuation from a checkpoint cannot agree with full replay in general. Two concurrent creates that minted one key go to whichever replay applies second in canonical causal order (crates/beadroll-core replay/apply/create.rs), so a late older-id create keeps the key in a full replay and is renamed in a continuation. Comments, claim history, lost claims and issue order are replay order. What a checkpoint can offer is that every machine continuing from the same checkpoint agrees: the checkpoint is canonical and the archive stops being an oracle.
- Events behind the boundary can still be causes: a late event's deps are the frontier it saw, and write_register, dep_remove, label removal and the claim rules ask saw_at(event, old id). A checkpoint keeps an index over all history (id to chain and position, and the clocks), or declares such events unmergeable.
- Receipts: settle_commands (crates/beadroll-sync/src/ownership.rs) recognises an accepted attempt by its file in claims/. A retry after compaction must still recognise an attempt accepted before it.
- Rollback to python-0.1.0 (docs/REVIEWING.md §2, docs/RUST-PORT.md §2.3j) ends for a rolled-over tracker, and the fork, quarantine and chain-break findings in docs/FINDINGS.md assume every raw record is present.

The deliverable is a docs/REVIEWING.md §2 row and a README paragraph: the boundary (none; or a window, and in what: events, segments, days), what a machine behind it sees (the error code and what bead tells it to do), what happens to its pending work, which of the properties above change and which tests pin them today. Also the shape of the retention question (step 6), so that step 5 leaves room for it. Informed by step 3's number: how often a merge on a real tracker brings concurrent events, which bounds how often a continuation would differ from a replay.

Step 4 of the epic. Waits for step 3.
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- docs/REVIEWING.md §2 has the row: the decision, the alternatives considered and why, and the tests that pin today's behaviour with what changes for them.
- README.md says what a user sees at the boundary, or that there is none.
- On main.
fields.title: Decide the history boundary: arbitrarily old offline work, or a supported window with explicit reconciliation

fields.description:
The last mechanism, and only when a real tracker hurts. The published tree carries every segment and attempt file, the remote ref every sync's commit (259 commits for 762 events on this repository's tracker; 28 MB of loose objects after 1,000 changing syncs, 852 KB after gc, in docs/FINDINGS.md), and a fresh machine fetches all of it with no depth limit (the fetch in crates/beadroll-sync/src/link.rs). Rotation reduces none of it, and the projection (step 3) changes nothing in what is published.

What it would be:
- A checkpoint in the published tree: the state, the ancestry index (id to chain and position, and the clocks; about 100 bytes an event) and the accepted attempt ids (a receipt is recognised by its file in claims/), written by one writer at a known frontier and continued from by everyone, as step 4 decided.
- A bounded recent journal: the segments after the checkpoint's frontier. Older segments move to an archive ref, fetched on demand (bead log, an export of history, a machine behind the boundary).
- A rollover: a new live history on the ref, fenced against stale writers. The fence exists: a plain fast-forward push refuses a stale writer against an orphan root, and the manifest's format turns an old bead away with FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED (roll-dih8.7 is the upgrade story). The rollover itself is a one-time non-fast-forward update of the ref, which the design has avoided so far (README: a plain fast-forward push cannot truncate history); it needs its own coordination, and the archive pushed before it.
- Format 2: format 1 is frozen, so a tree with a checkpoint is a new format, with roll-dih8.7's upgrade path and the end of the python-0.1.0 rollback for that tracker, recorded.

The trigger is measured, not guessed: a real tracker whose published tree, remote ref or first fetch is a cost someone notices; write the numbers here when it happens. This repository's tracker at its busiest rate adds about 320 MB of journal and 33,000 commits a year (packed with deltas, a fraction of that), and a fresh machine's first sync after 1,000 syncs took 0.25 s (docs/FINDINGS.md). None of it hurts yet.

Step 5 of the epic. Waits for steps 3 and 4.
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- The trigger: a real tracker's measured cost, recorded here, that steps 1 to 3 did not remove.
- Differential tests over the stress models: continuation from a checkpoint equals full replay on every history without late concurrent events, and on histories with them every machine agrees with every other, the property step 4 decided.
- A retry recognises an attempt accepted before the checkpoint, with a failpoint test.
- A stale writer (an old bead, or an old head after the rollover) is refused, never merged silently and never dropped, with a failpoint test.
- A fresh machine's first fetch costs in proportion to the checkpoint and the recent journal, recorded by cargo xtask timing.
- Format 2 is documented with its upgrade path; docs/REVIEWING.md §2, README.md, docs/FINDINGS.md and CHANGELOG say what changed; the fast baseline and ./check.sh --stress green.
fields.title: Published checkpoints, an archive ref and a format-2 rollover, when a real tracker's tree or first fetch hurts

fields.description:
Compaction keeps every issue's current text, and on this repository's tracker the latest field values and the comments are 56% of the journal's bytes: a checkpoint halves it at best. Reclaiming more means forgetting closed issues, their comments and their history after some age. That is a product decision, not a storage one: it changes what bead show, bead log and bead export return, and breaks the Beads export round trip for the pruned issues (the compat tests and check.sh --real pin it today).

If it is ever wanted: a policy set explicitly per tracker (at bead init or by a setting, never a default), a command that prunes and lists what it forgot, an archive that still holds it (step 5's archive ref), and a documented effect on export. Not before step 5, and not folded into it.

Step 6 of the epic. Waits for step 5.
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- A docs/REVIEWING.md §2 row decides whether to offer it at all, from a measured need.
- If offered: the policy is explicit and off by default; the pruning command lists what it forgot and the archive keeps it; README.md says what export omits; the compat tests cover a pruned tracker.
fields.title: Retention: forgetting closed history is a separate, explicit policy

data.text: Step 1 of epic roll-lqjj (moved there from roll-dih8; priority raised to P2 to match). Measured on this repository's tracker on 2026-10-11: events average 3,503 bytes of JSON (creates 7.9 KB, sets 9.7 KB, comments 2 KB), so 200,000 real-shaped events are 700 MB raw, and the 150 MB budget on the synthetic shape (xtask's "note N" and "issue N" events) does not bound the real one. Whoever takes this: also record a real-shaped measurement (the generator given realistic text sizes, or this tracker's journal repeated to 200,000 events), because step 3, the projection (roll-lqjj.2), builds on this representation and needs to know it. Meeting 150 MB on the real shape means not holding events after they are applied, only the state and the ancestry index, which is more than sharing keys; whether to go that far is this issue's call, with the number written here either way. Step 3 waits for this issue; step 2, hashing only the active segment (roll-lqjj.1), does not.

Implemented on branch roll-lqjj-proportional-cost (delivered as a PR, the user's direction of 2026-10-11). The memo is sync.git/journal-memo (beadroll_store::Memo): per journal file its identity on disk when hashed (length, mtime and ctime to the ns, inode, device, as git's index compares; length alone would trust a fork the published copy replaced at the same length), its lines and its blob. A merge compares a remembered blob with the published one as it is; a publish names it in its tree only when the link made it or the merged tip's tree holds it at that path, because a gc drops a blob no ref reaches (V8's prune loop) and a tree naming it fails every mktree after (tested: memo::a_remembered_blob_sync_git_lost_is_hashed_again fails without that check). Segment lines come from the memo too, and repair_tail reads only the last byte of a whole segment, so a sync no longer reads every segment. cargo xtask timing --sync N, release, this Mac: 200k plain events, 207 segments: sync 3.43 s with the memo, 3.49 s without; rotated at 4 MiB (18 segments): 3.37 s / 3.40 s; 50k: 0.89 s / 0.97 s; 200k ownership-heavy (91,952 attempt files): 11.2 s / 14.2 s. The figure does not grow with full segments; it grows with events (3.9x for 4x): three loads and replays per sync (view before and after, merge's chain-break check), step 3's, plus per-file listing, stat and tree work over every attempt file, step 5's.

data.reason: A publish hashes only the journal files that changed since bead last hashed them: sync.git/journal-memo remembers each file's identity on disk, lines and blob; a remembered blob goes into a tree only when the link made it or the merged tip's tree holds it at that path, with a full rehash when a tree still cannot be made (L02). Tests: beadroll-sync memo:: (rotation, repaired tail, claim, tree equal without the memo, missing/stale/unreadable memo, blobs lost to gc). cargo xtask timing --sync: at 200k events the sync no longer grows with full segments (3.43 s with 207, 3.37 s with 18); 92k attempt files save 3 s a sync. ./check.sh --stress green; Codex review clean after fixing L01 and L02. On branch roll-lqjj-proportional-cost, PR https://github.com/bpcakes/beadroll/pull/1 (reaches main when merged).

data.text: Decision of 2026-10-12 (the user, in the session implementing epic roll-lqjj): the 150 MB budget at 200,000 events is met on the allocator-counted heap peak for both shapes, which cargo xtask timing records beside the RSS peak; the RSS gap goes to a follow-up issue. Why: after the compact representation (journal 546 -> ~96 MB heap, replayed state 260 -> ~100 MB) the heap peak is 141 MB plain and 160 MB ownership-heavy, but RSS stays at 221 and 266 MB because the system allocator barely reuses the memory replay frees (the journal's) for the state it builds: RSS is about the journal at load plus everything replay allocates. Reaching 150 MB RSS would need a ~3x smaller state as well, or another allocator. Remaining work here: compact dependency tags, claim history, replay temporaries and the journal index; heap peak in timing.

fields.acceptance_criteria: cargo run --release --package xtask -- timing --replay 200000 records a resident peak (peak_bytes) of at most 150 MB for both shapes (plain and --ownership), with every suite green; or a decision in docs/REVIEWING.md §2 that the heap peak is the budget for good, with its reason.
fields.title: Replay's resident peak at 200,000 events within 150 MB, as its heap peak is

data.text:
Measured 2026-10-12 on this Mac with `cargo run --release --package xtask -- timing --replay N [--ownership]` (release build, best of seven). The heap peak is the most the `timing --load` process held on its heap at once, counted by xtask's allocator; the resident peak is what /usr/bin/time reports for the same process.
- 200,000 plain: replay 0.21 s; heap peak 107 MB (the journal alone 92 MB); resident 187 MB (108 MB).
- 200,000 ownership-heavy (110,374 of them in attempt files): replay 0.29 s; heap peak 133 MB (116 MB); resident 215 MB (143 MB).
Both meet the 150 MB budget on the heap, as decided above. The resident gap is roll-dih8.15.

Real shape: this tracker's journal (292 events averaging 1,078 bytes of JSON today: creates 1.6 KB, sets 2.1 KB, comments 1.3 KB; the planning comment's 3,503 bytes an event is about three times that), repeated to 200,120 events. Each copy has ids and keys of its own and builds on the one before (36,882 issues, 206 MB of segments). It peaks at 364 MB on the heap, 245 MB of it the loaded journal, and at about 470 MB resident. The texts are most of it, and the journal and the state both hold them.

This issue's call on the real shape: it stops at the compact representation and does not drop events once applied. The local projection (roll-lqjj.2) makes a whole-journal replay the exception, and it needs to keep only the state and the ancestry index. The figures are in docs/RUST-PORT.md Appendix A.

data.reason: Replay of 200,000 events now holds at most 107 MB on the heap (plain) and 133 MB (ownership-heavy), recorded by cargo xtask timing --replay beside the resident peaks, which fell from 921/958 MB to 187/215 MB; replay 0.21/0.29 s. A journal keeps what replay reads of each event and a digest of its content, not its JSON, with repeated texts and values once and objects boxed; replay takes each event's operation and the state keeps who wrote it and what it had seen, not the journal; issues keep registers, tags and claims in small vectors, claim records share names and derive times, clocks are positions alone, deps are a view, the frontier is computed on demand. Real shape (this tracker repeated to 200,120 events): 364 MB heap. Resident gap: roll-dih8.15. Commits 93028e8, 9986eed, ede58be, 7d8e623, de78a9b, 2a86d22, ef7fec6 on branch roll-lqjj-proportional-cost (PR #1); fast baseline green; Codex review clean in round 1.

data.text:
For step 4, the fraction of merges on this repository's tracker that brought concurrent events: none. On 2026-10-12 the tracker held 299 events, all written on one machine (194cc432) by agents taking the store lock in turn, and no two of them are concurrent: for every pair, one is in the other's past (its causes, followed back). So no merge has brought another machine's events at all, let alone ones written concurrently with this store's, and the projection would have taken every write and merge in without a replay. A busier tracker of two machines would answer otherwise; the measure is every pair of events checked for being in neither one's past.

Measured with the projection on this Mac (`cargo xtask timing --read/--merge/--sync`, best of five, docs/RUST-PORT.md Appendix A): at 200,000 events a read (list, show, ready) takes 73–87 ms where replaying took 1.06 s; on a thousand issues changed over and over it takes 18 ms at 50,000 events and at 200,000 (replay: 0.22 and 0.85 s). A sync that merges ten events another machine wrote after the frontier takes 0.31 s (1.31 s without the projection); on the churn history 90 ms at 50,000 events and 109 ms at 200,000, and 118 ms for a hundred events. A publishing sync takes 0.38 s (1.34 s without the projection, 1.45 s without it or the memo). What still grows with the events: the 16-byte id of every event the projection keeps to tell held records from new ones, and every journal file stat'd on each command, which a store of 92,000 attempt files pays for (a read there takes 0.56 s, where replaying took 3.5 s).

data.reason: Every command reads <store>/projection (the replayed state, keyed by the bead build and every journal file's identity as read, with a sum of each segment) instead of replaying the whole journal; records appended to a machine's last segment and new attempt files are applied after it when replay would apply them so (each new event has the whole frontier in its past), anything else replays. Answers are replay's: differential tests over three-machine histories that write, sync and race, hostile batches, damaged/cut/foreign/missing projections, a write that fails and a bead killed as it writes one. Merges append what another machine's segment lacks; the unpublished count reads segments through the memo; Tx applies emitted events lazily. At 200k events: reads 73-87 ms (cold 1.06 s), 18 ms on a thousand issues at 50k and 200k events; a merge of ten 0.31 s (cold 1.31 s); a publishing sync 0.38 s (1.34 s without the projection). This tracker: no merge has brought concurrent events (one machine, 299 events). Docs: README, REVIEWING §2, RUST-PORT §1.1 and Appendix A, CHANGELOG, FINDINGS L03-L06. ./check.sh --stress green; Codex review clean in round 3. Branch roll-lqjj-proportional-cost (PR #1).

fields.description:
Measured on 2026-10-12 for roll-lqjj.3 (docs/RUST-PORT.md, Appendix A, "roll-lqjj.3: real trackers, migrated"): a read decodes the whole projection and a write rewrites it, both in proportion to the state, and a real tracker's state is mostly its text. Descriptions and comments are 64-81% of it; on the largest public Beads trackers closed issues hold 27-83% of the bytes.

- The six largest public Beads trackers (21-47 MB, 1,300-13,394 issues), imported: a read takes 58-138 ms warm holding 109-274 MB, 0.22-0.57 s cold; a published write 0.34-0.65 s; a sync with nothing to do 0.18-0.37 s.
- 30 times the maintainer's busiest tracker (6,810 issues, 60 MB of journal): a write 0.68 s, a read 0.11 s holding 304 MB, where they take 0.15 s and 21 ms at its size.

The projection made a command cost what the state does (roll-lqjj.2); for real trackers that is still most of what the history wrote, since the texts are kept. Direction: keep texts out of what every command decodes and rewrites: an index of issues with their texts read on demand (show reads one issue's, list and ready none), and a write that adds what changed instead of rewriting the whole file. Measure first with cargo xtask timing on a text-heavy history (a real tracker's text repeated), since the synthetic histories carry little text.
fields.acceptance_criteria: A read that prints no text (list, ready) and a local write cost in proportion to the issues' other fields and the change, not to the texts, recorded by cargo xtask timing on a text-heavy history at 200,000 events, with the figures before and after. The projection stays a cache (deleting it is safe; another build's is never read), format 1 untouched, and the differential tests against replay unchanged. README's known limits and docs/RUST-PORT.md Appendix A updated.
fields.title: Commands cost in proportion to all issue text: keep texts out of what every command decodes and rewrites

fields.description:
Measured on 2026-10-12 for roll-lqjj.3 (docs/RUST-PORT.md, Appendix A): four machines writing one tracker at once in a sandbox, each write publishing to a local bare remote. Every view converged; a write took 161 ms at the median, but 14 of 200 took over a second, the worst 22.7 s, and one was left unpublished after twelve rounds. Two machines: 5 of 100 over a second, the worst 6.2 s. Against GitHub a round takes about 1-1.7 s, so the window in which another machine wins the race is wider.

This is how bead is used: the maintainer's dealsafe is developed on up to four machines at once with an orchestrator, and the heaviest public Beads users have hundreds of agent names on one tracker. docs/REVIEWING.md section 2 decided that the store lock is held while a sync or claim pushes and that publishing is serialised on one ref, and README's known limits record claims at 9 s median under four machines syncing continuously; this asks whether those decisions still hold for writes at this concurrency.

Directions to weigh: a lost race means another machine published, so the next round has events to merge but need not back off as long; a machine's queued writes going out in one push; pushing outside the store lock; per-machine refs that readers merge (a format question).
fields.acceptance_criteria: Four machines writing one tracker continuously, against a remote with a realistic round-trip time, measured by cargo xtask timing or a stress test: writes' median, p99 and how many were left unpublished, before and after. Any change keeps every machine converging (the stress models and the protocol sweep green) and is recorded in docs/REVIEWING.md section 2 beside the decisions it revisits; README's known limits say what remains.
fields.title: Several machines writing at once: publishes contend on one ref, and a write can take 20 s or stay unpublished

fields.description:
roll-lqjj.2's projection takes new records in only when each new event has every head in its past; a merge that brings events written concurrently with the store's replays the whole journal. Measured on 2026-10-12 for roll-lqjj.3 (docs/RUST-PORT.md, Appendix A): on the one bead tracker two machines write, 31 of 303 merges (10%) brought concurrent events, and with four machines writing at once nearly every publish does.

Today this costs little: a real tracker's state is most of its journal, so a replay costs about what an extension does (0.45 s against a 0.68 s write at 30 times the busiest tracker). Once a command stops costing the whole text (the follow-up on text), every concurrent merge costs a whole-history replay. Taking concurrent events in without replaying needs replay's order-dependent outcomes reproduced: the key rename between two concurrent creates, the order of comments, claim history and issue order. That is the question a checkpoint's continuation faces too (roll-lqjj.4; docs/REVIEWING.md section 2, the history-boundary row).

Trigger: the text follow-up done, or a tracker whose replay passes half a second while most of its merges bring concurrent events.
fields.acceptance_criteria: Either the projection takes merges with concurrent events in, its state equal to replay's in the differential tests over every interleaving of the stress models' histories, concurrent ones included; or the measured cost of replaying on them, at the sizes the text follow-up leaves, is recorded as acceptable in docs/REVIEWING.md section 2.
fields.title: A merge that brings concurrent events replays the whole journal, which is common where several machines write

fields.description:
Measured on 2026-10-12 for roll-lqjj.3 (docs/RUST-PORT.md, Appendix A): bead init --import of the largest public Beads tracker (47 MB, 13,394 issues) took 4.0 s and held 951 MB resident; trackers of 21-35 MB held 330-523 MB. On the same tracker a new machine's first sync held 494 MB, and a read without the projection 496 MB.

An import holds the parsed records, the events it plans, the journal it writes, the replay that follows and the projection at once. Find where the peak is (cargo xtask timing's heap counting, on a generated large export), and bring it down where that is cheap: records dropped once planned, the plan written as it is made. A memory budget for import is the maintainer's to set.
fields.acceptance_criteria: The peak of importing a generated 50 MB export is measured and recorded (docs/RUST-PORT.md Appendix A), where it goes is known, and it meets the budget the maintainer sets; the import stays all or nothing.
fields.title: Import holds about twenty times the tracker's size: 951 MB for a 47 MB Beads export

data.text:
Decision (the maintainer, 2026-10-12): no history boundary. Offline work of any age merges by itself; a checkpoint, when step 5 comes, carries the id index over all history and the accepted attempt ids, and continuation from it is the reference for late concurrent events (every machine continuing from one checkpoint agrees). Recorded in docs/REVIEWING.md section 2; README says there is no boundary.

How it was decided: the maintainer asked twice for more evidence before choosing, first from all of their Beads trackers, then beyond their own usage, since beadroll is open source. The evidence, with method and numbers, is docs/RUST-PORT.md Appendix A, "roll-lqjj.3: real trackers, migrated":
- 22 Beads trackers of the maintainer's (19 repositories) and the six largest public ones on GitHub (21-47 MB, 1,300-13,394 issues) imported into sandboxes: every record round-trips but for an empty comments list, a second machine agrees every time.
- 18 git histories replayed as bead commands: 7,826 events, journal 1.1-2.9 times the state, the projection's index 22-30 bytes an event.
- 849 public repositories' tracker histories read from blobless clones; branch-held tracker changes waited up to 258 days (over 30 days in 4 of the 51 that merge tracker changes).
- the bead stores in use: one merge in ten brought concurrent events where two machines write; four sandbox machines writing at once converge, with a tail up to 23 s and one write left unpublished.
- prior art: Automerge keeps full history; Sync Framework's forgotten knowledge forces a recovery sync; CouchDB's revision limit and Riak's clock pruning trade old work for spurious conflicts.

Follow-ups filed under the epic from the same evaluation: roll-lqjj.6 (texts in every command), roll-lqjj.7 (contended publishing), roll-lqjj.8 (replay on concurrent merges), roll-lqjj.9 (import memory).

Correction (2026-10-12): the planning figures in this description ("this repository's own tracker: 250 issues, 762 events, 2.6 MB of journal, 262 events a day at the busiest, 259 commits on the remote ref") were measured on the store of another repository's tracker (batter's, the one tracker two machines write), not this repository's. This repository's tracker held 301 events and 325 KB on 2026-10-12. They remain a fair figure for a busy real tracker. roll-lqjj.3's evaluation (docs/RUST-PORT.md Appendix A) measured more: the largest public Beads trackers are 21-47 MB with up to 13,394 issues, and four follow-ups came out of it: roll-lqjj.6 to roll-lqjj.9.

Measured trigger status, 2026-10-12 (roll-lqjj.3's evaluation, docs/RUST-PORT.md Appendix A): not reached for the maintainer's trackers (under 3 MB of journal each; a new machine's first sync 77-151 ms from a local remote). The heaviest public Beads trackers are close: the largest imports as 29,046 events and 55 MB of journal, all of it in the published tree, and a new machine's first sync takes 1.8 s from a local remote holding 494 MB; its own timestamps show 50,000 creates, closes and comments a year before any update, so its tree would pass a few hundred MB within about a year. The trigger stands as written (a real tracker's tree, ref or first fetch that someone notices); for heavy multi-agent users expect it within a year.

roll-lqjj.3 decided no history boundary: the checkpoint carries the id index over all history (22-30 bytes an event, measured in the projection) and the accepted attempt ids; continuation from it is canonical, so the differential tests here check that every machine continuing from one checkpoint agrees, and that continuation equals replay on histories without late concurrent events (one merge in ten brings them where two machines write).

Measured need, 2026-10-12 (roll-lqjj.3's evaluation, docs/RUST-PORT.md Appendix A): on the largest public Beads trackers closed issues hold 27-83% of the state's bytes, and issues closed more than 30 days before the tracker's last update 5-79%; descriptions and comments are 64-81% of the state. Every command decodes the state and every write rewrites it, so retention would cut most of a mature tracker's per-command cost. roll-lqjj.6 (keeping texts out of what every command decodes) would remove most of that cost without forgetting anything, so it comes first: the trigger here is a tracker whose state or published tree still hurts after roll-lqjj.6 and roll-lqjj.4, or users asking to forget.
The text follow-up named in the description is roll-lqjj.6.

fields.description:
Found on 2026-10-12 by roll-lqjj.3's evaluation (docs/RUST-PORT.md, Appendix A): recent Beads versions keep memory records in .beads/issues.jsonl beside the issues, one JSON object a line of the shape {"_type": "memory", "key": "...", "value": "..."}, with no "id". bead's import checks a file whole and refuses it at the first such line:

  VALIDATION: issues.jsonl:1897: record has no string 'id'

so a tracker that holds even one memory cannot be imported at all. The largest public Beads tracker on GitHub (48.5 MB) holds 1,111 of them beside 3,578 issues, and GitHub's code search finds the exact "_type":"memory" in about a hundred public trackers' issues.jsonl (of some 3,300 it indexes). With the memory lines set aside, that tracker imports and round-trips like the others.

The choice is the maintainer's; bead never guesses at unknown input and never half-writes:
- carry them: import keeps each record whose "_type" it does not handle as an opaque record of the tracker (an additive operation in format 1; an older bead sets it aside), and export writes them back after the issues, so the file round-trips;
- refuse with a precise message and an explicit way past it (an import flag that leaves such records out and lists how many, or a documented jq filter), nothing written otherwise;
- both: carry memories, refuse any other "_type".
A related, smaller difference: export writes every dependency with br's six members, so a dependency bd wrote without thread_id comes back with "thread_id": "" (2,103 and 2,392 records of the two bd-written trackers); Beads readers accept it, and README could say so.
fields.acceptance_criteria: A Beads export with memory records imports, or is refused with a message that says what to do, as the maintainer decides; either way nothing is half-written, a compat test covers a file with memory records, and README says what happens to them on import and export.
fields.title: Import refuses a Beads export that holds memory records (_type: memory), so recent Beads trackers cannot migrate

fields.description:
Measured on 2026-10-12 for roll-lqjj.3 (docs/RUST-PORT.md, Appendix A, "roll-lqjj.3: real trackers, migrated"): a read decodes the whole projection and a write rewrites it, both in proportion to the state, and a real tracker's state is mostly its text. Its texts (descriptions, designs, notes, comments) are most of it; on the largest public Beads trackers closed issues hold 27-100% of the bytes.

- The eight largest public Beads trackers (21-49 MB, 1,300-13,394 issues), imported: a read takes 58-138 ms warm holding 109-284 MB, 0.18-0.57 s cold; a published write 0.34-0.65 s; a sync with nothing to do 0.18-0.37 s.
- 30 times the maintainer's busiest tracker (6,810 issues, 60 MB of journal): a write 0.68 s, a read 0.11 s holding 304 MB, where they take 0.15 s and 21 ms at its size.

The projection made a command cost what the state does (roll-lqjj.2); for real trackers that is still most of what the history wrote, since the texts are kept. Direction: keep texts out of what every command decodes and rewrites: an index of issues with their texts read on demand (show reads one issue's, list and ready none), and a write that adds what changed instead of rewriting the whole file. Measure first with cargo xtask timing on a text-heavy history (a real tracker's text repeated), since the synthetic histories carry little text.

Measured on 2026-10-12 for roll-lqjj.3 (docs/RUST-PORT.md, Appendix A): bead init --import of a 47 MB public Beads tracker (13,394 issues, the most of any) took 4.0 s and held 951 MB resident; trackers of 21-46 MB held 313-575 MB. On the same tracker a new machine's first sync held 494 MB, and a read without the projection 496 MB.

A memory budget for import is the maintainer's to set.

data.reason: Each issue's texts are kept apart from the projection's state in <store>/projection-texts, read in only where a command prints them: list, ready, blocked, claims, dep, writes and syncs read none, show/comments/update/claim/takeover only their issues', export/search/lint all. Measured (docs/RUST-PORT.md Appendix A): text-heavy history at 200,000 events, reads 144-159 -> 72-82 ms, a local write 188 -> 92 ms, projection 107 -> 20 MB (what a history without texts takes); largest public Beads tracker (47 MB): list 138 -> 75 ms, resident 274 -> 98 MB, a published comment 0.65 -> 0.35 s. Codex review 10: round 1 one finding (L07, texts read once per record, fixed), round 2 clean. Commits b60b680..8f74e62 on branch roll-lqjj-follow-ups (PR #2).

Measured with cargo xtask timing --contend (new): four machines publishing every write at once against a remote taking 0.3 s a fetch or a push converge every time; before, 2 of 650 writes were left unpublished after twelve rounds. The maintainer's decision (2026-10-12): tune today's protocol, correctness before speed, a write over a second is no defect. A sync or ownership command now makes 24 rounds, waiting any time up to 0.1 x 2^(attempt-1) s, at most 2 s, between them: none of 650 writes left unpublished, longest waits shorter, medians within noise. Recorded in docs/REVIEWING.md section 2, docs/RUST-PORT.md section 1.3, section 5 row 19 and Appendix A, README known limits, CHANGELOG. Stress and the full protocol sweep green. Codex review 10, roll-lqjj.7 round 1: clean. Commits 4691b15..0147312 on branch roll-lqjj-follow-ups (PR #2).

Kept a replay, by the maintainer's direction (correctness before speed), on the acceptance's second way: the cost of a merge that brings concurrent events, measured with cargo xtask timing --merge N --concurrent (added), is a replay: 0.45 s at 50,000 events, 1.0-2.0 s at 200,000 (plain, text-heavy, churn), where a merge after everything takes 0.10-0.40 s; about a merge in ten where two machines write. Recorded as acceptable in docs/REVIEWING.md section 2 with why (reproducing replay's order-dependent outcomes without replaying is the question a checkpoint's continuation faces), docs/RUST-PORT.md Appendix A, README known limits, CHANGELOG. data.text: Decision (maintainer, 2026-10-12): the import memory budget is 'no worse than a cold start': an import's heap peak stays within what making the projection of the imported journal takes (the first sync after an offline import); a published import peaks at that making. Not chosen: a fixed 256 MB; 200 MB (needs the projection's making cut); 100 MB for the import alone (planner moving records, the transaction keeping journal lines). Measured with cargo xtask timing --import 14000 (generated 49.4 MB export; heap counted by cargo xtask bead, bead run in xtask's counting process): offline 473 -> 165 MB heap (651 -> 300 MB resident), published 473 -> 245 MB (802 -> 549 MB), the first sync after an offline import 309 -> 245 MB. Public trackers of 21-47 MB: offline 72-172 MB against 101-235 MB for their projection's making. Commits 0c7e8bd (the tool), 20560a0 (the fixes), 7c86d70 (docs: REVIEWING section 2, RUST-PORT Appendix A, README, changelog).

data.reason: An import holds each form of its export once (0c7e8bd the measuring tool, 20560a0 the fixes, 7c86d70 the docs): the export's text until its records are read, the records until planned, each event once and let go of as it is encoded; init reads the prefix before importing; a text file is written from its parts. A generated 49 MB export peaks at 165 MB on the heap offline (473 before) and 245 MB published, the projection's making, which meets the maintainer's budget of 2026-10-12 (no worse than a cold start); public trackers of 21-47 MB at 72-172 MB against 101-235 MB. cargo xtask timing --import records it, counting bead's heap through cargo xtask bead. Recorded in docs/REVIEWING.md section 2 and docs/RUST-PORT.md Appendix A; fast and stress baselines green; Codex's first review clean.
